identity: A school-reader anthology of Arabic children's verse (Ahmad Shawqi's poems for children), flattened into one unbroken paragraph with no <NL> at all. Ten titled pieces run together: al-Hirra wa-l-nazafa, al-Jadda, al-Watan ('usfuratani fi l-Hijaz), al-Rifq bi-l-hayawan, al-Umm, Walad al-ghurab, al-Nil, al-Madrasa, Nashid Misr, Nashid al-kashshafa. Every piece is fully metrical and monorhymed or stanza-rhymed; the register is didactic and declamatory, not prose. Because the text is verse, it carries its own segmentation signal: the rhyme word.
law: The sentence unit is the BAYT (the complete metrical verse, sadr + 'ajuz), closed by the rhyme word; and each poem's TITLE is a unit of its own. Two negative clauses do the real work. (1) Never cut at a hemistich (shatr) boundary: hemistichs in this corpus are routinely syntactically incomplete, so a shatr-level law would sever verb from object and oath from imperative. (2) Never cut inside a bayt, even where a clause plainly finishes mid-verse. Where the meter is muzdawij (al-Rifq bi-l-hayawan) or murabba'/musammat (al-Nil, Nashid Misr, Nashid al-kashshafa), the bayt is still two ashtur, so each AAAB stanza yields TWO boundaries, not four: the third A-shatr closes the first bayt's 'ajuz only when it is the second shatr of that bayt. Syntactic completeness is the tie-breaker for confidence, never for placement: a bayt end stays a boundary even under enjambment, and a syntactic close mid-bayt is never a boundary.
reasoning: Unit test, shatr vs bayt. I resolved this at four sites where the two laws disagree, and all four kill the shatr: 'nabtadiru l-khayra wa-nastabiq | ma yurda l-khaliqu wa-l-khalq' (a shatr cut severs verb from object); 'ya Rabbi bi-'Isa wa-l-Hadi | wa-bi-Musa khudh bi-yadi l-watan' (severs the oath from its imperative); 'hiya ma lam tataharrak | dumyatu l-bayti l-zarifa' (severs subject+protasis from predicate); 'al-bahru l-fayyadu l-qudus | al-saqi l-nasa wa-ma gharasu' (the shatr alone is a bare apposition). Hence bayt. Stanzaic poems. al-Nil, Nashid Misr and Nashid al-kashshafa are murabba'/musammat with rhyme AAAB. I read each stanza as TWO abyat, not four short lines, on the same non-severance test: 'jarun wa-yura laysa bi-jar | li-anatin fihi wa-waqar' -- the second half is a causal PP, not a sentence, so the four-line reading is wrong. Meter confirms it: each of these short lines is one shatr (four feet of khabab / majzu' al-rajaz), so a bayt is two of them. Walad al-ghurab. I counted 18 rhyme positions in -qi and had to decide whether muzaqqaq (351) is a tasri' of the opening sadr (giving 9 abyat) or a real qafiya (giving 18). Syllable count settles it: 'wa-mumahhadin fi l-wakri min waladi l-ghurabi muzaqqaqi' scans as four mutafa'ilun, a full bayt of majzu' al-kamil, and 'ka-ruwayhibin mutaqallisin muta'azzirin mutanattiqi' scans identically. So 18 abyat. Titles. All ten are confirmed internally by echo in the first line (al-Nil / 'al-Nilu l-'adhbu huwa l-kawthar'; al-Madrasa / 'ana l-madrasa'; Nashid al-kashshafa / 'nahnu l-kashshafa'; Walad al-ghurab / 'wa-mumahhadin fi l-wakri min waladi l-ghurab'), which also rules out reading the title tokens as part of the following verse. A heading cannot be continuous with the verse under it, so each is a boundary. Enjambment sites, kept as boundaries but downgraded. These are the places where the bayt law and a syntax law part company, and I am flagging them so a grade can tell me which law this corpus actually holds. lo: 46 (kullama ... al-mutifa needs its answer ghasalathu in the next bayt), 155 ('ala fanan / fi khamilin' -- PP runs on), 169 (bayna huma ... needs marra), 189 ('ra'aytu ... 'Adan / khama'ila' -- object follows), 255 (appositive list mid-flight), 351 and 355 (the rubba-clause still has no predicate), 483 (appositive series), 689 (fa-lamma has no apodosis until nasha'na), 773 (one long vocative list). med: quotation-introducing verses (133, 222, 448), simile chains (323, 329, 336, 361), coordinated wa-sami'tu / wa-ra'aytu / wa-'araftu clauses (430, 436), and list closes (259, 490, 526, 595, 602, 779, 830, 838). If the gold turns out to be syntax-driven rather than verse-driven, these are exactly the boundaries to drop, and nothing else changes. hi elsewhere: bayt end and full syntactic close coincide, which is the overwhelming majority -- these poems are end-stopped by design. Index 869 (al-watan) is the guaranteed final-token boundary and closes Nashid al-kashshafa on its refrain.
